doc.title: John Altman interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 14, 2023

title: Mini-movies and decoding ad agency requests
summary: He scored mini-movies for famous directors and learned to interpret vague requests like a jazz track; funny studio anecdotes.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: Ah, you’re anticipating a question I’m going to ask later about music and emotions and all that, but I wanted to talk briefly about — do you call them jingles?

Yeah they can be. I don’t feel that I was particularly a jingle composer, although I have written a couple that have been successful on that front. But mainly there was all the mini-movies with directors like Ridley Scott, Hugh Hudson, Alan Parker, John Frankenheimer, and then great photographers like Elliot Erwitt and David Bailey and Terrence Donovan. And my lyricist on a few was Salmon Rushdie.
Oh my God. Well I’m talking about selling products.
Yeah. So if a representative of an ad agency is having a meeting with you and they’re selling paper towels, did you have to learn how to interpret the way they spoke about music into actual music?

Oh absolutely. And I think very helpful for that was my academic background in English literature. Because I was always looking to try and comprehend subtext of anything that people said. And what was always very interesting was you would often get people saying, “I want a jazz track.” And that could mean Louis Armstrong or it could mean Ornette Coleman. You know, I want something classical. Is that Bach or is that Stravinsky? I want country & western. Do you mean a hoedown or do you mean Dolly Parton? It’s very interesting. You are constantly trying to narrow people’s focus. So if I would go in for a meeting, and you would, you know, sometimes get “Could you make it green?” or I mean you get some very funny comments that I tried to keep away from the musicians because they would all burst out laughing. So I would try to keep them out of the control room. I mean one when they actually did come in, sadly, was for processed cheese. And I said to the director, “What do you think?” He said, “Well I may be wrong but it seems to start at the beginning and go all the way through very nicely until the end, when it stops.” I said, “Yes, that’s about the only way I know how to write music I’m afraid. But you know he’s chording a lot on the bottom string and somebody said to the © Fillius Jazz Archive -8-
guitarist, “If I heard a noise in my head could you play it?” And he said, “Well actually I had five years medical training, I could probably cure it.”
